subject: Science
cluster: PS2 Motion and Stability: Forces and Interactions (PS2.A Forces and Motion, PS2.B Types of Interactions)
text: Plan and conduct an investigation to provide evidence of the effects of balanced and unbalanced forces on the motion of an object.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can design an experiment to test how different forces affect the motion of an object and explain my findings with clear evidence. Example: I can create a ramp, roll a ball down, and change the angle to show how a steeper ramp increases speed, explaining the forces at play.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can explain how balanced and unbalanced forces affect the motion of an object, providing examples of each. Example: I can describe how pushing a box harder makes it move faster (unbalanced force) compared to when no one is pushing it (balanced forces).
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can identify that pushes and pulls affect the motion of objects, but I need help explaining balanced and unbalanced forces. Example: I know that when I push a swing, it moves, but I can’t describe how different strengths of pushes change its motion.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can say that things move when I push or pull them, but I don’t explain how forces work. Example: I notice that pushing a toy car makes it move, but I can’t explain why.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: PS2 Motion and Stability: Forces and Interactions (PS2.A Forces and Motion)
text: Make observations and/or measurements of an object’s motion to provide evidence that a pattern can be used to predict future motion.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can conduct an experiment to investigate motion patterns and use data to accurately predict how changes in force affect the motion of an object. Example: I can vary the strength of my push on a toy car and graph the distances it travels, explaining how the force changes its motion.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use observations to identify patterns in the motion of objects and make predictions about their future motion. Example: I can explain that a ball will roll farther if I give it a stronger push.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can describe some patterns in the motion of objects, but I need help predicting future motion based on those patterns. Example: I can say that a toy car rolls down a hill, but I can't predict how far it will go.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can notice that objects move, but I don’t explain how to predict their motion. Example: I see a ball rolling, but I can't say why it rolls in a certain direction.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: PS2 Motion and Stability: Forces and Interactions (PS2.B Types of Interactions)
text: Ask questions to determine cause and effect relationships of electric or magnetic interactions between two objects not in contact with each other.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can design and conduct an investigation to explore electric or magnetic interactions, formulating questions and drawing conclusions based on my observations. Example: I can create a simple circuit to show how electric forces can make a light bulb light up and explain the cause-and-effect relationship.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can explain how electric or magnetic forces cause objects to move without touching and provide examples of such interactions. Example: I can describe how two magnets can push apart or pull together even when they are not touching.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can identify that some forces can act at a distance, but I need help explaining how electric and magnetic forces interact. Example: I know that a magnet can pull a metal object closer, but I can’t describe the force involved.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can notice that some objects can move without touching, but I don’t explain how this happens. Example: I see magnets attract paper clips but can’t say why.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: PS2 Motion and Stability: Forces and Interactions (PS2.B Types of Interactions)
text: Define a simple design problem that can be solved by applying scientific ideas about magnets.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can use my model to explain how changes in temperature affect the movement of particles in different states of matter. Example: I can demonstrate how heating water molecules causes them to move faster and change from liquid to gas, explaining the particle behavior involved.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can develop a model to show that matter is made of particles and explain how these particles are arranged in different materials. Example: I can create a diagram showing that ice, water, and steam are all made of water molecules, which are arranged differently.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can describe that matter is made of tiny pieces, but I need help explaining how these particles interact. Example: I can say that water is made of small bits, but I can’t explain how they fit together.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can say that things are made of smaller parts, but I don’t explain what those parts are. Example: I know that a rock is solid, but I can’t say what it’s made of.

descriptor_flag: School descriptor may not match this standard

descriptors_suggested.cc_advanced: I can define a magnet design problem with clear criteria and constraints and explain how magnet ideas help solve it.
descriptors_suggested.cc_at_target: I can define a simple design problem that can be solved using what I know about magnets.
descriptors_suggested.cc_approaching: I can describe a problem a magnet could solve, like keeping a door closed, with a template.
descriptors_suggested.cc_emerging: I can show that a magnet sticks to some objects.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: LS1 From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes (LS1.B Growth and Development of Organisms)
text: Develop models to describe that organisms have unique and diverse life cycles but all have in common birth, growth, reproduction, and death.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can analyze and compare the life cycles of various organisms, constructing detailed models that highlight their unique features and commonalities, and explain the importance of each stage. Example: I can present a comprehensive model comparing the life cycles of plants and animals, explaining how each stage contributes to their survival and reproduction.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can develop models to show the life cycles of different organisms, identifying the common stages of birth, growth, reproduction, and death. Example: I can create a diagram showing the life cycle of a butterfly and a frog, pointing out their similarities and differences.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can describe some stages of life cycles for certain organisms, but I need help explaining the differences and similarities across species. Example: I can say that frogs have eggs and tadpoles, but I can’t compare this to how butterflies grow.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can say that living things grow and change, but I don’t explain how they do this. Example: I know that plants start as seeds, but I can’t describe what happens next.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: LS2 Ecosystems: Interactions, Energy, and Dynamics (LS2.D Social Interactions and Group Behavior)
text: Construct an argument that some animals form groups that help members survive.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can analyze various animal group behaviors and construct a detailed argument that explains the survival advantages of these groups, supported by evidence. Example: I can compare the survival strategies of different animals, like schools of fish and herds of zebras, and explain how their grouping behaviors enhance their chances of survival.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can construct an argument explaining how grouping helps some animals survive, using examples from nature. Example: I can argue that wolves hunt in packs to catch prey more effectively and protect each other.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can describe that animals form groups, but I need help explaining the benefits of grouping for survival. Example: I can say that birds fly in flocks, but I can’t explain how this helps them avoid danger.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can notice that some animals are in groups, but I don’t explain why they do this. Example: I see that fish swim together, but I can’t say how it helps them.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: LS3 Heredity: Inheritance and Variation of Traits (LS3.A Inheritance of Traits, LS3.B Variation of Traits)
text: Analyze and interpret data to provide evidence that plants and animals have traits inherited from parents and that variation of these traits exists in a group of similar organisms.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can interpret complex data sets to demonstrate how traits are inherited and analyze variations, providing evidence for my conclusions. Example: I can compare genetic traits in different animal breeds and explain the inheritance patterns and variations observed.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can analyze data to show that plants and animals inherit traits from their parents and identify variations within a group. Example: I can examine a chart of different flower colors in a plant species and explain how these traits are inherited.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can describe that traits can be inherited and identify some variations, but I need help analyzing data. Example: I can say that some plants have different leaf shapes, but I can’t explain the reasons for these differences.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can identify that traits are passed from parents to offspring but can’t explain how this happens. Example: I notice that kittens look like their parents but can’t say why.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: LS3 Heredity: Inheritance and Variation of Traits (LS3.A Inheritance of Traits, LS3.B Variation of Traits)
text: Use evidence to support the explanation that traits can be influenced by the environment.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can analyze and synthesize evidence to support detailed explanations of how environmental changes influence traits across various organisms. Example: I can provide examples of how pollution affects the coloration of animals and explain the biological mechanisms involved.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use evidence to support explanations of how traits can be influenced by environmental factors. Example: I can explain how temperature affects the color of leaves in certain plants using examples from my observations.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can describe that environmental factors can affect traits but need help providing specific examples. Example: I can mention that animals may change color in different seasons but can’t explain the reasons.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can say that traits can be influenced by the environment but don’t explain how this works. Example: I know that some plants grow taller in the sun but can’t say why.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: LS4 Biological Evolution: Unity and Diversity (LS4.A Evidence of Common Ancestry and Diversity)
text: Analyze and interpret data from fossils to provide evidence of the organisms and the environments in which they lived long ago.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can interpret fossil data to reconstruct ancient ecosystems and discuss how they have changed over time. Example: I can create a project showing how different fossils indicate changes in climate and habitat over millions of years.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can analyze fossil data to identify organisms and describe the environments they lived in. Example: I can look at a fossil and explain what type of animal it was and where it might have lived.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can describe what fossils are but struggle to connect them to ancient environments. Example: I can say that fossils are remains of old plants or animals.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can explain what fossils are or why they are important. Example: I don’t know what a fossil tells us about the past.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: LS4 Biological Evolution: Unity and Diversity (LS4.B Natural Selection)
text: Use evidence to construct an explanation for how the variations in characteristics among individuals of the same species may provide advantages in surviving, finding mates, and reproducing.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can analyze evidence and construct a detailed explanation of how specific variations provide advantages in different environments. Example: I can discuss how long necks in giraffes help them reach leaves in tall trees, giving them an advantage in their habitat.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use evidence to explain how variations in characteristics can help individuals survive. Example: I can explain that a rabbit’s fur color can help it hide from predators.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can describe some differences among individuals in a species but struggle to connect them to advantages. Example: I can say that some dogs are big and some are small but don’t explain why that matters.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can’t explain what variations in characteristics are. Example: I don’t know how animals in the same species can look different.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: LS4 Biological Evolution: Unity and Diversity (LS4.C Adaptation)
text: Construct an argument with evidence that in a particular habitat some organisms can survive well, some survive less well, and some cannot survive at all.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can analyze multiple pieces of evidence to construct a detailed argument about survival in various habitats and discuss adaptations. Example: I can argue that polar bears survive in the Arctic due to their thick fur and fat, while other animals struggle to live there.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can construct an argument using evidence to explain why certain organisms thrive while others do not in a specific habitat. Example: I can explain that cacti survive well in the desert because they store water, while other plants do not.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can describe that some organisms are better suited for their habitats but struggle to provide evidence. Example: I can say that fish live in water, but I can’t explain why.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can’t explain why some organisms survive better than others. Example: I don’t know why some animals live in certain places and others don’t.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: LS4 Biological Evolution: Unity and Diversity (LS4.D Biodiversity and Humans)
text: Make a claim about the merit of a solution to a problem caused when the environment changes and the types of plants and animals that live there may change.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can analyze different solutions to environmental problems and articulate their merits based on evidence. Example: I can discuss how creating protected areas for wildlife can help preserve species affected by habitat loss and explain why this is important.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can make a claim about a solution to a problem caused by environmental changes and give reasons for my claim. Example: I can argue that planting more trees can help improve air quality for animals.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can describe that changes in the environment can affect living things but struggle to suggest solutions. Example: I can say that pollution makes it hard for fish to live, but I don’t know how to help.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can’t explain how environmental changes affect plants and animals. Example: I don’t know what happens when a forest is cut down.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: ESS2 Earth's Systems (ESS2.D Weather and Climate)
text: Represent data in tables and graphical displays to describe typical weather conditions expected during a particular season.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can analyze weather data and create detailed graphical displays, explaining the significance of the patterns observed. Example: I can create a graph showing temperature changes over the seasons and explain why certain weather patterns occur.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can represent weather data in tables and simple graphs to describe typical conditions for a season. Example: I can create a chart showing the average temperatures and rainfall for winter.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can collect some weather data but struggle to organize it. Example: I can say it rained last week, but I don’t know how to show that on a chart.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can’t represent weather data or describe typical conditions. Example: I don’t know how to show what the weather is like in a season.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: ESS2 Earth's Systems (ESS2.D Weather and Climate)
text: Obtain and combine information to describe climates in different regions of the world.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can analyze and compare climates from various regions, discussing how they affect the environment and living things. Example: I can compare the climate of a rainforest to that of a tundra and explain how each supports different types of plants and animals.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can obtain and combine information to describe climates in different regions, including temperature and precipitation. Example: I can explain that tropical climates are warm and wet, while polar climates are cold and dry.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can identify some climates but have difficulty combining information about them. Example: I can say that it’s hot in the desert, but I can’t explain other climates well.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can’t describe different climates or where they are found. Example: I don’t know what climate means or how it's different in various places.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: ESS3 Earth and Human Activity (ESS3.B Natural Hazards)
text: Make a claim about the merit of a design solution that reduces the impacts of a weather-related hazard.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can analyze multiple design solutions, discussing their merits and drawbacks in reducing impacts from weather-related hazards. Example: I can compare different strategies, like building storm shelters and improving drainage systems, and explain how each can help during severe storms.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can make a claim about a design solution that helps reduce the impacts of a weather-related hazard and provide reasons for my claim. Example: I can argue that building levees can help protect homes from flooding.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can identify a weather-related hazard but struggle to suggest solutions to reduce its impacts. Example: I can say that floods can be harmful, but I don’t know how to prevent them.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can’t explain what a weather-related hazard is or how it affects people. Example: I don’t know what a hurricane is or why it’s dangerous.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: PS3 Energy (PS3.A Definitions of Energy)
text: Use evidence to construct an explanation relating the speed of an object to the energy of that object.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can apply my understanding to real-life situations and explain how speed and energy affect safety or design. Example: I can explain why cars need stronger brakes when going downhill because they have more energy at higher speeds.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use evidence to explain that the faster an object moves, the more energy it has. Example: I can explain that a fast-moving soccer ball has more energy because it travels farther when kicked.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can recognize that faster objects seem to have more energy, but I need help explaining why. Example: I notice a fast ball makes a louder sound when it hits something, but I’m not sure what that means about energy.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can describe that objects move, but I’m not sure how speed and energy are connected. Example: I can say a car moves fast, but I can't explain why that means it has more energy.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: PS3 Energy (PS3.A Definitions of Energy, PS3.B Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer)
text: Make observations to provide evidence that energy can be transferred from place to place by sound, light, heat, and electric currents.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can connect what I know about energy transfer to explain how it powers or changes things in the real world. Example: I can explain how solar panels collect light energy and change it into electricity to power homes.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can make observations and use evidence to show that energy is transferred by sound, light, heat, or electricity. Example: I can explain that a light bulb lights up because electric energy is transferred through the wire.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can notice that energy moves, but I need help explaining how or where it goes. Example: I can say a pan gets hot on the stove, but I’m not sure how the heat moves into it.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can name types of energy like sound or light but need help understanding how they move or transfer. Example: I know light comes from a flashlight, but I can’t explain how the energy moves.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: PS3 Energy (PS3.A Definitions of Energy, PS3.B Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer, PS3.C Relationship Between Energy and Forces)
text: Ask questions and predict outcomes about the changes in energy that occur when objects collide.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can explain how energy changes during collisions and connect it to real-world situations like sports or car crashes. Example: I can explain how energy is transferred when a hockey puck is hit and why it slows down after hitting the goalpost.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can ask questions and predict how energy changes when objects collide. Example: I can ask what happens when a fast-moving ball hits a still one and predict that energy will make the second ball move.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can ask questions about what happens during a collision, but I need help predicting energy changes. Example: I can wonder why one ball moves faster after hitting another, but I’m not sure why.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can tell when objects hit each other, but I don’t understand how energy is involved. Example: I can say two balls bumped, but I can’t explain what changed.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: PS3 Energy (PS3.B Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer, PS3.D Energy in Chemical Processes and Everyday Life)
text: Apply scientific ideas to design, test, and refine a device that converts energy from one form to another.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can improve a device and explain how it converts energy more efficiently or in new ways. Example: I can design a solar-powered fan and explain how it changes light energy into electrical, then into motion.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use scientific ideas to design and test a device that changes energy from one form to another. Example: I can build a simple circuit that turns electrical energy into light or sound and explain how it works.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can describe a simple device that uses energy, but I need help designing or explaining how it changes energy. Example: I can say a toaster uses electricity, but I’m not sure how it turns into heat.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can talk about different types of energy, but I need help thinking of how to change one type into another. Example: I know a flashlight uses batteries, but I don’t know how the energy changes.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: PS4 Waves and Their Applications in Technologies for Information Transfer (PS4.A Wave Properties)
text: Develop a model of waves to describe patterns in terms of amplitude and wavelength and that waves can cause objects to move.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can create and explain models that compare different types of waves and predict how they affect motion in real life. Example: I can model sound and water waves and explain why a boat rocks more in bigger waves.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can make a model of a wave to show its amplitude and wavelength and explain how waves can cause objects to move. Example: I can show that a bigger wave (higher amplitude) can move a ball more than a smaller wave.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can show what a wave looks like and name parts like crest or trough, but I need help describing how waves move or affect things. Example: I can label a wave diagram, but I’m not sure how waves make things move.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can say what a wave is, but I don’t understand what amplitude or wavelength mean. Example: I can draw waves, but I can’t explain what the parts mean or what they do.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: PS4 Waves and Their Applications in Technologies for Information Transfer (PS4.B Electromagnetic Radiation)
text: Develop a model to describe that light reflecting from objects and entering the eye allows objects to be seen.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can explain real-life situations where light reflection helps us see and apply that to design or solve problems. Example: I can explain how mirrors work by reflecting light and design a periscope to see around corners.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can make a model to show that light bounces off objects and enters the eye so we can see them. Example: I can show with a diagram that light reflects from a book and travels to my eyes so I can see it.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can say that light helps us see, but I need help explaining how it reflects and enters the eye. Example: I know a flashlight helps in the dark, but I’m not sure how the light helps me see the object.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can say that I see things with my eyes, but I don’t understand how light helps me see. Example: I know I can see a pencil, but I don’t know light is involved.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: PS4 Waves and Their Applications in Technologies for Information Transfer (PS4.C Information Technologies and)
text: Generate and compare multiple solutions that use patterns to transfer information.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can create and compare real-life ways people use patterns to send information and explain why one way might work better. Example: I can compare Morse code and binary code to decide which is better for fast communication.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can make and compare different solutions that use patterns to send messages. Example: I can create a pattern of light flashes or sounds to send a message and explain how it works.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can recognize that patterns can be used to send messages, but I need help creating or comparing them. Example: I can say Morse code is a way to send messages, but I can't make or explain it clearly.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can name an example of sharing information, but I don’t yet understand how patterns help transfer it. Example: I know people use phones to talk, but I don’t know how it works.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: LS1 From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes (LS1.A Structure and Function)
text: Construct an argument that plants and animals have internal and external structures that function to support survival, growth, behavior, and reproduction.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can explain how internal and external structures work together in real life and give examples from different animals or plants. Example: I can explain how a bird’s hollow bones and wings help it fly to find food and escape predators.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can explain how different body parts help plants and animals survive, grow, and reproduce. Example: I can explain how a fish's gills help it breathe underwater and fins help it swim.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can describe how some body parts help plants or animals live, but I need help explaining how they work together. Example: I can say that roots help a plant get water, but I’m not sure how that helps the plant grow.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can name a part of a plant or animal, but I don’t know what it does to help it survive. Example: I know birds have wings, but I’m not sure why that’s important.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: LS1 From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes (LS1.D Information Processing)
text: Use a model to describe that animals receive different types of information through their senses, process the information in their brain, and respond to the information in different ways.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can use a model to explain real-life situations where animals use senses and brain signals to survive, and compare different responses. Example: I can explain how both a deer and a rabbit react differently to danger using their senses and brain signals.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use a model to show how animals use their senses, send the information to the brain, and respond in different ways. Example: I can draw a diagram of a cat hearing a noise, its brain processing it, and then running away.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can describe that animals get information through senses and respond, but I need help showing how the brain is involved. Example: I can say a dog hears a sound and barks, but I’m not sure how its brain helps.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can say animals use their senses, but I’m not sure how they respond to what they sense. Example: I know animals can hear, but I don’t know what happens after they hear a sound.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: ESS1 Earth's Place in the Universe (ESS1.C The History of Planet Earth)
text: Identify evidence from patterns in rock formations and fossils in rock layers to support an explanation for changes in a landscape over time.

descriptors.cc_advanced: Synthesizes multiple pieces of evidence from rock formations and fossil records to make a well-supported, detailed explanation of complex landscape changes across time periods. Example: A student compares different fossil layers and erosion marks in rocks to explain a multi-phase transformation from ocean to riverbed to desert, citing specific fossil types and rock features.
descriptors.cc_at_target: Clearly identifies evidence from patterns in rock layers and fossils to construct a logical explanation of landscape changes over time. Example: A student explains that layers with fish fossils below layers with plant fossils indicate that the area changed from a sea to a land environment.
descriptors.cc_approaching: Identifies simple patterns in rock formations or fossils and gives a basic explanation of how they suggest a change in the landscape. Example: A student observes a seashell fossil in a rock found inland and says the area “used to be under the sea.”
descriptors.cc_emerging: Recognizes that rocks and fossils provide clues about the past but needs support to describe specific patterns or changes in landscapes. Example: A student can point to a fossil in a picture and say it is “from a long time ago” but cannot explain what it tells us about the land.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: ESS2 Earth's Systems (ESS2.A Earth Materials and Systems, ESS2.E Biogeology)
text: Make observations and/or measurements to provide evidence of the effects of weathering or the rate of erosion by water, ice, wind, or vegetation.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can use real data and detailed observations to explain how different forces cause erosion or weathering at different speeds. Example: I can compare how fast wind moves sand dunes versus how slow plant roots break rocks.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can make observations or take measurements to show how weathering or erosion changes land over time. Example: I can observe how rain wears down soil on a hill and describe the change.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can describe how water, wind, or ice can change land, but I need help making or using observations. Example: I can say waves change the beach, but I need help showing or measuring it.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can name things like wind or water, but I don’t understand how they change the land. Example: I know rivers flow, but I don’t know they can shape the land.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: ESS2 Earth's Systems (ESS2.B Plate Tectonics and Large-Scale System)
text: Analyze and interpret data from maps to describe patterns of Earth’s features.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can analyze different kinds of maps to explain how and why Earth’s features form patterns, and connect them to natural events. Example: I can explain how earthquakes often happen near mountain ranges shown on a map.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use maps to find and describe patterns in Earth’s features, like where mountains, rivers, or deserts are located. Example: I can say that mountains are often in long lines near the edges of continents.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can find some land or water features on a map, but I need help explaining the patterns. Example: I can point to mountains on a map but can’t say why they are grouped in certain places.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can look at a map, but I don’t understand what the features or symbols mean. Example: I see mountains and rivers on the map, but I don’t know what they show.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: ESS3 Earth and Human Activity (ESS3.A Natural Resources)
text: Obtain and combine information to describe that energy and fuels are derived from natural resources and that their uses affect the environment.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can explain how different energy sources affect the environment and suggest ways we can use cleaner or renewable energy. Example: I can compare solar and fossil fuels and explain why solar energy is better for the environment.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can gather and combine information to explain that energy and fuels come from natural resources and using them changes the environment. Example: I can describe how coal comes from the ground and burning it causes air pollution.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can say that energy comes from natural things and it can change the environment, but I need help explaining the details. Example: I can say burning fuels can cause pollution, but I can’t explain how or why.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can name some sources of energy like gas or sunlight, but I don’t know where they come from or how they affect the Earth. Example: I know we use gas for cars, but I don’t know where it comes from.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: ESS3 Earth and Human Activity (ESS3.B Natural Hazards)
text: Generate and compare multiple solutions to reduce the impacts of natural Earth processes on humans.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can compare real-life solutions to natural disasters and explain which ones work best in different places or situations. Example: I can explain why early warning systems work well for tsunamis and how they save lives
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can come up with and compare different ways to reduce the effects of natural events on people. Example: I can compare building sea walls to raising homes to prevent flood damage.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can suggest one way to stay safe during a natural event, but I need help thinking of more or comparing them. Example: I can say people can move away from flood areas, but I can’t explain other options.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can name a natural disaster like a flood or earthquake, but I don’t know how people can stay safe from it. Example: I know earthquakes happen, but I don’t know what people can do about them.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: PS1 Matter and Its Interactions (PS1.A Structure and Properties of Matter)
text: Develop a model to describe that matter is made of particles too small to be seen.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can develop and use a model to explain real-world phenomena by describing how matter's invisible particles behave and interact. For example, I can create a model to explain how the smell of cookies baking spreads through a room by showing the movement and diffusion of invisible scent particles through the air particles.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can develop a model to describe that matter is made of particles too small to be seen. For example, I can draw a diagram showing sugar dissolving in water, with tiny, invisible sugar particles spreading out among the equally tiny, invisible water particles.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can say that matter is made of small pieces, but I struggle to create a model that shows these particles are too small to be seen or how they behave. For example, I might draw very large dots to represent sugar dissolving in water, making them seem visible.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can state that objects are made of "stuff" but cannot describe it as particles. For example, I can say a table is made of wood, but I can't explain that the wood is made of tiny, invisible pieces.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: PS1 Matter and Its Interactions (PS1.A Structure and Properties of Matter, PS1.B Chemical Reactions)
text: Measure and graph quantities to provide evidence that regardless of the type of change that occurs when heating, cooling, or mixing substances, the total weight of matter is conserved.
ee_text: Target Level: Measure and compare weights of substances before and after heating, cooling, or mixing substances to show that weight of matter is conserved. Precursor Level: Compare the weight of an object before and after it changes from a liquid to a solid and from a solid to a liquid. Initial Level: Recognize the change in state from liquid to solid or from solid to liquid of the same material.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can design an investigation, accurately measure and graph quantities, and use the evidence to explain and defend the principle that the total weight of matter is conserved in various transformations, relating it to everyday situations. For example, I can explain that when sugar dissolves in tea, the total weight of the sweetened tea is the sum of the tea and the sugar, even though the sugar is no longer visible.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can measure and graph quantities to provide evidence that regardless of the type of change that occurs when heating, cooling, or mixing substances, the total weight of matter is conserved. For example, I can weigh an ice cube, let it melt, weigh the water, and create a graph showing the weight remained constant.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can measure the weight of substances before and after a change, but I may not consistently find the weight is conserved or I struggle to represent this with a graph. For example, I might weigh an ice cube and then the water after it melts, but my graph might not clearly show the weights were the same.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can observe changes in matter, like ice melting, but I don't connect this to measuring weight or the idea that weight stays the same. For example, I can watch an ice cube turn into water but not think about weighing it before and after.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can weigh substances before and after heating, cooling, or mixing and show that the weight stays the same.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: PS1 Matter and Its Interactions (PS1.A Structure and Properties of Matter)
text: Make observations and measurements to identify materials based on their properties.
ee_text: Target Level: Make observations and measurements to identify materials based on their properties (e.g., weight, shape, texture, buoyancy, color, or magnetism). Precursor Level: Classify materials by physical properties. (e.g., weight, shape, texture, buoyancy, color, or magnetism). Initial Level: Match materials with similar physical properties.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can systematically test and compare multiple properties of various materials to identify them and then justify why certain materials are chosen for specific real-world applications based on those properties. For example, I can test copper, plastic, and wood for conductivity and explain why copper is used for wires and plastic for wire insulation.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can make observations and measurements to identify materials based on their properties. For example, I can test unknown materials for properties like color, hardness, reflectivity, electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity, response to magnetic forces, and solubility to identify them.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can observe and make simple measurements of some properties (like hardness or if it dissolves in water) but may not use enough different properties to reliably tell materials apart. For example, I might test if two white powders dissolve in water but not test other properties to distinguish them.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can describe one or two obvious properties of a material, like its color, but I don't use these to identify it. For example, I can say a substance is white but not use other properties to figure out if it's salt or sugar.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can observe and measure materials (weight, shape, texture, floating, color, magnetism) to identify them.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: PS1 Matter and Its Interactions (PS1.B Chemical Reactions)
text: Conduct an investigation to determine whether the mixing of two or more substances results in new substances.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can design and conduct an investigation, carefully observing and recording multiple signs of a chemical reaction (e.g., gas production, temperature change, color change, precipitate formation) to conclude whether new substances are formed, and can relate this to everyday examples of chemical changes. For example, I can explain how cooking an egg changes its properties, indicating new substances are formed, by observing changes in texture, color, and state.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can conduct an investigation to determine whether the mixing of two or more substances results in new substances. For example, I can mix baking soda and vinegar, observe the production of gas and a change in temperature as evidence that a new substance has formed.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can mix substances and notice some changes (like a color change), but I am unsure how to tell if these changes mean a new substance with different properties has actually formed. For example, I might see fizzing when I mix two things but not know if that means it's a new material.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can mix substances together but do not look for specific evidence to decide if a new substance has formed. For example, I can stir salt and water but not observe if it looks different or if something new was made.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: PS2 Motion and Stability: Forces and Interactions (PS2.B Types of Interactions)
text: Support an argument that the gravitational force exerted by Earth on objects is directed down.
ee_text: Target Level: Demonstrate that the gravitational force exerted by Earth on objects is directed down. Precursor Level: Predict the direction an object will go when dropped. Initial Level: Recognize the direction an object will go when dropped.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can construct a robust argument, using diverse evidence from everyday phenomena, to demonstrate that Earth's gravitational force is consistently directed "down" (towards Earth's center) and apply this understanding to explain why objects behave as they do in various real-world contexts. For example, I can explain that a plumb bob always points "down" towards the Earth's center, helping builders make straight walls, because of gravity's consistent downward pull, regardless of where on a building they are.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can support an argument that the gravitational force exerted by Earth on objects is directed down. For example, I can explain that no matter how I drop a ball or throw it up, it always comes back towards the ground, showing evidence that gravity pulls things "down."
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can state that gravity pulls objects down, but I find it hard to use examples or observations to clearly support an argument about the direction of this force. For example, I know a dropped apple falls, but I struggle to explain how this specific observation proves the force is always "down."
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can observe that objects fall to the ground, but I cannot explain why or in what specific direction a force is acting. For example, I see a ball drop but don't connect it to a specific force called gravity or its consistent direction.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can show that Earth's gravity pulls objects down.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: PS3 Energy (PS3.D Energy in Chemical Processes and Everyday Life)
text: Use models to describe that energy in animals’ food (used for body repair, growth, motion, and to maintain body warmth) was once energy from the sun.
ee_text: Target Level: Create a model to describe that energy in animals' food was once energy from the Sun. Precursor Level: Use models to describe that plants capture energy from sunlight. Initial Level: Identify simple models that show that plants need sunlight to grow.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can create and explain detailed models (like food webs) to trace the flow of energy from the sun through multiple organisms in an ecosystem, explaining how all animal life ultimately depends on solar energy for survival and bodily functions. For example, I can design a food web for a local pond and explain how the sun's energy supports everything from algae to fish to herons, and how this energy allows them to live and grow.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use models to describe that energy in animals’ food (used for body repair, growth, motion, and to maintain body warmth) was once energy from the sun. For example, I can draw a food chain (sun -> grass -> cow -> human) and explain how the sun's energy flows through it, enabling the human to move and grow.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can describe that animals get energy from eating plants or other animals, but I struggle to clearly model or explain how this energy ultimately traces back to the sun. For example, I can draw a picture of a rabbit eating a carrot for energy, but I'm unsure how to show the sun's role in the carrot's energy.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can say that animals eat food to get energy, but I cannot explain where the food's energy originally comes from or use a model to show this. For example, I know a cat eats fish to run, but I don't know how the sun is involved.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can make a model that shows the energy in animals' food first came from the sun.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: LS1 From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes (LS1.C Organization for Matter and Energy Flow in)
text: Support an argument that plants get the materials they need for growth chiefly from air and water.
ee_text: Target Level: Provide evidence that plants need air and water to grow. Precursor Level: Provide evidence that plants grow. Initial Level: Distinguish things that grow from things that don’t grow.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can construct a detailed argument, citing experimental evidence (like Van Helmont's experiment or data about photosynthesis), to convincingly demonstrate that plants primarily build their mass from carbon dioxide in the air and water, and can relate this to the process of photosynthesis and its importance for producing food for ecosystems. For example, I can explain that a large tree gets most of its mass from the air and water, not by "eating" the soil, and this is how it makes its own food.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can support an argument that plants get the materials they need for growth chiefly from air and water. For example, I can explain that while plants use soil for small amounts of nutrients, most of their actual substance for growing bigger comes from carbon dioxide in the air and water absorbed by their roots, using evidence from experiments that show soil mass doesn't decrease much as plants grow.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can say that plants need air, water, and soil to grow, but I struggle to clearly argue or provide evidence that air and water are the chief materials for their growth (their mass). For example, I know plants need water from the soil and air to "breathe," but I think the soil provides most of what makes them get bigger.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can state that plants need soil to grow, but I cannot explain that their main materials for building their bodies come from air and water. For example, I think plants "eat" soil like animals eat food.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can show evidence that plants need air and water to grow.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: LS2 Ecosystems: Interactions, Energy, and Dynamics (LS2.A Interdependent Relationships in Ecosystems, LS2.B Cycles of Matter and Energy Transfer in Ecosystems)
text: Develop a model to describe the movement of matter among plants, animals, decomposers, and the environment.
ee_text: Target Level: Create a model that shows the movement of matter (e.g., plant growth, eating, composting) through living things. Precursor Level: Identify a model that shows the movement of matter from plants to animals (e.g. food chain/food web). Initial Level: Identify common human foods.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can design and explain a comprehensive model illustrating how specific types of matter (like carbon or nitrogen at a basic level) cycle through an ecosystem, detailing the crucial roles of plants (producers), animals (consumers), and especially decomposers in returning essential materials to the environment for reuse, and can predict impacts of disruptions to this cycle. For example, I can explain how if decomposers were removed from a forest, dead leaves and animals would pile up, and nutrients wouldn't return to the soil, affecting new plant growth and the entire food web.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can develop a model to describe the movement of matter among plants, animals, decomposers, and the environment. For example, I can draw a diagram showing a plant taking nutrients from the soil and air, an animal eating the plant, the animal dying, and decomposers (like fungi or bacteria) breaking it down to return nutrients to the soil and gases to the air.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can create a simple model showing animals eating plants, but I struggle to include decomposers or clearly show how matter cycles back into the environment (like soil or air). For example, I can draw a rabbit eating a carrot, but my model doesn't show how the carrot's matter eventually returns to the soil to help new carrots grow.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can describe that animals eat plants, but I cannot create a model to show how matter moves between plants, animals, decomposers, and the environment in a cycle. For example, I know a deer eats grass, but I don't know what happens to the deer's body or the grass's matter when they die.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can make a model that shows how matter moves through living things, such as plant growth, eating, and composting.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: ESS1 Earth's Place in the Universe (ESS1.A The Universe and its Stars)
text: Support an argument that differences in the apparent brightness of the sun compared to other stars is due to their relative distances from Earth.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can construct a well-reasoned argument, using analogies (like comparing the brightness of a nearby flashlight to a distant car headlight) and scientific understanding, to explain that distance is the primary factor determining the apparent brightness of stars, including our sun, and differentiate this from a star's actual luminosity. For example, I can explain that two identical streetlights will appear to have different brightnesses if one is close and one is far away, and this is similar to how we see the Sun versus distant stars.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can support an argument that the apparent brightness of the sun and stars is due to their relative distances from the Earth. For example, I can explain that even though many stars are much larger and hotter than our sun, they appear as tiny points of light because they are incredibly far away, while our sun appears very bright because it is much closer to Earth.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can say that the sun is closer than other stars, but I struggle to form a clear argument with examples to show that distance is the main reason for the sun's apparent brightness compared to other stars. For example, I know the Sun is our closest star, but I can't use an analogy like streetlights appearing dimmer further away to explain star brightness.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can state that the sun is bright and stars are less bright, but I cannot explain that this difference is mainly due to their distances from Earth. For example, I see the sun is much brighter than stars at night, but I think it's just because the sun is "bigger."

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: ESS1 Earth's Place in the Universe (ESS1.B Earth and the Solar System)
text: Represent data in graphical displays to reveal patterns of daily changes in length and direction of shadows, day and night, and the seasonal appearance of some stars in the night sky.
ee_text: Target Level: Represent and interpret data on a picture, line, or bar graph to show seasonal patterns in the length of daylight hours. Precursor Level: Recognize patterns about length of daylight hours over time (e.g., week to week, month to month). Initial Level: Order events in daily routine including sunrise and sunset.

descriptors.cc_advanced: Integrates multiple sets of data into graphical formats and provides a clear, detailed explanation of how these patterns reflect Earth’s rotation and orbit. Example: A student presents two graphs, one of shadow lengths over a day and one of daylight hours across months, and explains how both are connected to Earth’s movement relative to the sun.
descriptors.cc_at_target: Accurately represents observational data in a graph or chart and uses it to explain patterns in shadow length, daylight duration, or star visibility across seasons. Example: A student produces a line graph showing how a shadow gets shorter at midday and explains that the sun is highest at that time.
descriptors.cc_approaching: Collects basic data about shadows or sky observations and attempts to organize it into a simple graph or table. Example: A student creates a bar graph showing the length of a shadow at morning, noon, and afternoon but offers only a limited explanation of the pattern.
descriptors.cc_emerging: Recognizes that shadows and the appearance of the sky change over time but requires support to organize or interpret data. Example: A student draws a picture of a shadow at different times but cannot label the times or explain the change.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can show and read daylight hours on a picture, line, or bar graph to find seasonal patterns.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: ESS2 Earth's Systems (ESS2.A Earth Materials and Systems)
text: Develop a model using an example to describe ways the geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere, and/or atmosphere interact.
ee_text: Target Level: Develop a model showing how water (hydrosphere) affects the living things (biosphere) found in a region. Precursor Level: Recognize how water (hydrosphere) affects people in a region (e.g., floods, droughts, mudslide, tourism, and recreation). Initial Level: Anticipates routine (e.g., clothes to wear, activities to do) to follow when it is raining.

descriptors.cc_advanced: Designs a complex model integrating all four Earth systems and clearly explains their dynamic interactions over time or due to human/environmental impact. Example: A student creates a diagram showing how deforestation (biosphere) affects soil erosion (geosphere), reduces cloud formation (atmosphere), and changes runoff patterns (hydrosphere), and explains the long-term consequences.
descriptors.cc_at_target: Creates a clear model showing how at least three of Earth’s systems interact in a specific natural event or process. Example: A student illustrates a forest ecosystem where rain (hydrosphere) erodes soil (geosphere) and affects plant life (biosphere), with a brief description of each interaction.
descriptors.cc_approaching: Develops a simple model (drawing or diorama) showing two Earth systems and describes a basic interaction. Example: A student draws a river (hydrosphere) watering trees (biosphere) and explains that “plants need water to grow.”
descriptors.cc_emerging: Names Earth's systems (e.g., water, land, air, life) with support but struggles to describe or show how they interact. Example: A student labels “water” and “plants” on a picture but doesn’t explain the connection between them.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can make a model that shows how water affects the living things in a place.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: ESS2 Earth's Systems (ESS2.C The Roles of Water in Earth’s Surface)
text: Describe and graph the amounts of salt water and fresh water in various reservoirs to provide evidence about the distribution of water on Earth.

descriptors.cc_advanced: Clearly explains the implications of Earth's water distribution for human use and supports this explanation with a well-structured graph and analysis. Example: A student graphs the data and explains that because most fresh water is frozen or underground, only a tiny amount is available for drinking, linking it to water conservation needs.
descriptors.cc_at_target: Accurately describes the global distribution of salt and fresh water and represents this data in a labeled graph or chart. Example: A student creates a bar graph showing oceans as 97% of Earth's water, glaciers as most of the freshwater, and lakes/rivers as a small fraction.
descriptors.cc_approaching: Describes the main types of water on Earth and attempts to represent their proportions in a simple chart. Example: A student creates a pie chart showing that oceans are the biggest source of water but doesn’t include percentages or details.
descriptors.cc_emerging: Identifies that water exists in different forms (e.g., ocean, river) but struggles to differentiate between salt and fresh water or represent this data. Example: A student says “the ocean is water” but doesn’t know it is salt water or how it compares to other water sources.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
cluster: ESS3 Earth and Human Activity (ESS3.C Human Impacts on Earth Systems)
text: Obtain and combine information about ways individual communities use science ideas to protect the Earth’s resources and environment.
ee_text: Target Level: Use information to describe how people can help protect the Earth's resources and how that affects the environment. Precursor Level: Compare two methods people can use to help protect the Earth's resources. Initial Level: Identify one way to protect a resource of Earth (e.g., put paper in the recycling bin).

descriptors.cc_advanced: Integrates information from diverse sources and explains in depth how science-based strategies are used by different communities to protect various environmental systems. Example: A student compares how two cities use renewable energy, one with solar panels and one with wind turbines, and explains how these reduce carbon emissions and preserve air quality.
descriptors.cc_at_target: Combines specific information from multiple sources to explain how communities apply science to solve environmental problems. Example: A student researches and describes how a coastal city uses technology to monitor water quality and adjust sewage treatment to protect marine life.
descriptors.cc_approaching: Describes a simple action a community takes to protect resources and makes a general connection to science. Example: A student explains that a local town uses recycling bins to reduce waste, linking it to the idea of reusing materials.
descriptors.cc_emerging: Identifies a basic environmental issue but needs support to explain how science is used to address it. Example: A student mentions “littering is bad” but does not describe how communities use science to reduce it.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can use information to tell how people protect Earth's resources and how this helps the environment.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
strand: Engineering, Technology, and Applications of Science
cluster: ETS1 Engineering Design (ETS1.A Defining Engineering Problems)
text: Define a simple design problem reflecting a need or a want that includes specified criteria for success and constraints on materials, time, or cost.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can describe a real-world design problem, list the success criteria and limits, and explain why they matter. Example: I can design a shelter for a small animal using recycled materials and explain why cost, time, and strength are important.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can clearly describe a design problem that includes what the solution should do and what limits I have. Example: I can explain I need to build a paper boat that floats using only 10 straws and 20 minutes.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can describe a problem and what I want to happen, but I need help thinking about limits like time or materials. Example: I want to make a bridge that holds weight but forget I only have straws and tape.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can say what I want to make, but I don’t think about what I’ll need or how it should work. Example: I say I want to build a tower but don’t think about how tall it should be or what materials I can use.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
strand: Engineering, Technology, and Applications of Science
cluster: ETS1 Engineering Design (ETS1.A Defining Engineering Problems)
text: Define a simple design problem reflecting a need or a want that includes specified criteria for success and constraints on materials, time, or cost.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can describe a real-world design problem, list the success criteria and limits, and explain why they matter. Example: I can design a shelter for a small animal using recycled materials and explain why cost, time, and strength are important.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can clearly describe a design problem that includes what the solution should do and what limits I have. Example: I can explain I need to build a paper boat that floats using only 10 straws and 20 minutes.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can describe a problem and what I want to happen, but I need help thinking about limits like time or materials. Example: I want to make a bridge that holds weight but forget I only have straws and tape.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can say what I want to make, but I don’t think about what I’ll need or how it should work. Example: I say I want to build a tower but don’t think about how tall it should be or what materials I can use.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
strand: Engineering, Technology, and Applications of Science
cluster: ETS1 Engineering Design (ETS1.A Defining Engineering Problems)
text: Define a simple design problem reflecting a need or a want that includes specified criteria for success and constraints on materials, time, or cost.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can describe the problem and include limits like cost, time, safety, and materials in detail. Example: “We need a slide for 10 kids at once, under $500, safe in hot weather, and quick to build.”
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can define a design problem with clear limits (what it needs to do and what makes it hard). Example: “We need a new slide that is safe, can fit many kids, and is not too expensive.”
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can describe a problem and one part of what makes it hard to solve, but I don’t explain all the needs. Example: “The slide is too short” but not thinking about making it safe or fun.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can say what the problem is but not explain clearly what needs to be fixed or improved. Example: “The playground is broken” but not saying which part or why it’s a problem.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
strand: Engineering, Technology, and Applications of Science
cluster: ETS1 Engineering Design (ETS1.B Developing Possible Solutions)
text: Generate and compare multiple possible solutions to a problem based on how well each is likely to meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can compare real-life solutions to a problem and explain which one works best and why, based on goals and limits. Example: I evaluate several shelter designs and explain which one keeps animals safe while using the fewest resources.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can think of different ways to solve a problem and compare them to see which one meets the criteria and limits best. Example: I compare two boat designs to decide which one floats better and uses fewer materials.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can share a few ideas to solve a problem, but I need help comparing them or checking if they meet all the requirements. Example: I give two ideas for a tower but don’t explain which one is better for staying under budget.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can come up with one idea to solve a problem, but I don’t think about how well it works or follow the rules. Example: I suggest building a paper bridge but don’t check if it can hold weight or fits the materials limit.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
strand: Engineering, Technology, and Applications of Science
cluster: ETS1 Engineering Design (ETS1.B Developing Possible Solutions)
text: Generate and compare multiple possible solutions to a problem based on how well each is likely to meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can make and compare several detailed solutions, explaining which is best with evidence. Example: “We could add two slides, or one spiral slide. Two slides are cheaper and safer, but the spiral slide saves space. Two slides are the best solution.”
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can think of two or more ideas and compare them based on what is most important. Example: “We could make the slide longer or add two slides. Adding two slides is better because it lets more kids play.”
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can give more than one idea but only explain why one might work. Example: “We could make the slide longer or add two slides, but I only talk about the longer one.”
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can think of one idea but not more, or I don’t compare it to other ideas. Example: “Make a longer slide.”

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

subject: Science
strand: Engineering, Technology, and Applications of Science
cluster: ETS1 Engineering Design (ETS1.B Developing Possible Solutions, ETS1.C Optimizing the Design Solution)
text: Plan and carry out fair tests in which variables are controlled and failure points are considered to identify aspects of a model or prototype that can be improved.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can design fair, repeated tests and explain how the results show what parts of my design should be improved or redesigned. Example: I test different parachutes by keeping the drop height the same and use results to improve the parachute’s shape and size.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can plan and do a fair test by changing one thing at a time and use the results to decide what needs to be improved. Example: I test two car ramps by only changing the slope and find out which one makes the car go faster.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can do a test and notice if something doesn’t work, but I need help keeping it fair or finding what to fix. Example: I see that my tower falls over, but I’m not sure which part caused the problem.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can test my idea, but I don’t control the variables or look for what went wrong. Example: I test my paper airplane but don’t fly it the same way each time or check why it didn’t fly far.

source: NGSS DCI Arrangements (Achieve 2013, nextgenscience.org AllDCI.pdf)

strand: Engineering, Technology, and Applications of Science
cluster: ETS1 Engineering Design (ETS1.B Developing Possible Solutions, ETS1.C Optimizing the Design Solution)
text: Plan and carry out fair tests in which variables are controlled and failure points are considered to identify aspects of a model or prototype that can be improved.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can design fair, repeated tests and explain how the results show what parts of my design should be improved or redesigned. Example: I test different parachutes by keeping the drop height the same and use results to improve the parachute’s shape and size.
